prohibited_recommendations: Do not lower blood pressure aggressively before treating a severe stenosis with an internal border-zone infarct pattern
Do not add anticoagulation: there is no embolic source and the mechanism is large-artery
Do not defer carotid revascularisation because the presentation is cognitive rather than motor, or because of age alone
Do not attribute an abrupt cognitive step to progression of a degenerative disease
required_recommendations: Refer without delay to the vascular team for carotid endarterectomy of the symptomatic 70-80% right ICA stenosis: the cognitive step three months ago is within the 6-month window, and endarterectomy is preferred over stenting at age 80 [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]

Lower blood pressure (156/80 mmHg) gradually with an individualised target until the stenosis is treated, avoiding systolic below about 120 mmHg and orthostatic hypotension; aim for below 130/80 mmHg after revascularisation [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Intensify lipid lowering to LDL below 70 mg/dL (current 88 mg/dL on atorvastatin 40 mg): atorvastatin 80 mg, adding ezetimibe if the target is not reached [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Continue single antiplatelet therapy; there is no indication for anticoagulation
Arrange occupational therapy and caregiver support for the dressing apraxia and topographical disorientation

avoided_actions.rationale: No rapidly progressive or fluctuating course and no episode suggesting seizures; EEG has no diagnostic role here.
No parkinsonism, fluctuations, hallucinations or dream enactment; a dopamine transporter scan does not address the vascular question.
No feature of Lewy body disease or autonomic failure; cardiac sympathetic imaging does not inform this diagnosis.
A decline with an abrupt vascular step, not a subacute multidomain syndrome: an untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune battery has no indication.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
A severe ipsilateral stenosis explains the infarct pattern; prolonged monitoring does not change management.

accepted: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type from severe symptomatic right internal carotid stenosis, with a haemodynamic (internal border-zone) component

differential.key_features: Would not produce a strictly unilateral distribution with an internal border-zone pattern, and the ECG shows sinus rhythm without atrial ectopy in a patient with documented sinus rhythm historically
Recall is cue-responsive, medial temporal lobes are preserved, and the visuospatial and apraxic deficits localise to the infarcted right parietal cortex
Fazekas 2 change is present but asymmetric and follows the stenosed side; the cortical and border-zone infarcts are the substrate
Apraxia is present but there is no alien limb, no myoclonus, no progressive asymmetric rigidity, and the deficits appeared abruptly
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: Laterality is a mechanism argument: infarcts confined to one hemisphere downstream of a severe ipsilateral stenosis are large-artery, whereas cardioembolism scatters across territories and hemispheres
The internal border-zone (rosary-like) pattern in the centrum semiovale is a haemodynamic signature and changes the blood-pressure strategy: perfusion depends on the stenosis until it is treated
A carotid bruit recorded in the notes for two years and never imaged is the failure this case is built on
Apraxia and topographical disorientation localise to right parietal cortex, matching the largest infarct, and their abrupt onset dates the step
Atherosclerotic stroke with LDL 88 mg/dL on a statin calls for LDL below 70 mg/dL, with ezetimibe added if the statin alone does not reach it

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Bruno Cattaneo is an 80-year-old retired shipyard welder with polyvascular atherosclerosis — coronary bypass at 68, claudication, and a long smoking history — who attends with his wife for cognitive assessment. Her account is of a gradual decline over two years with an abrupt deterioration three months ago, when over a single morning he became confused about the date and about which flat he lived in, and stayed noticeably worse afterwards. There was no weakness or speech loss on that day. Since then he has needed help dressing in the correct order, has twice put his shoes on the wrong feet, and no longer recognises his own street from the car. He remembers people and conversations when reminded of the setting. He has never had a documented stroke. His blood pressure runs at 150-160 systolic. He has a right carotid bruit that has been noted in his notes for two years without further imaging. His pulse is regular, and inpatient telemetry during his bypass admission twelve years ago showed sinus rhythm throughout. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations and no dream enactment.
